newsitem.title: USA: Dow sets fourth straight record high, dollar falls.
newsitem.headline: Dow sets fourth straight record high, dollar falls.

text.p: The Dow industrials Monday surged to a fourth consecutive closing high as Wall Street was optimistic that interest rates will keep falling and attract more funds to the stock market.
The dollar fell to a one-month low against the yen as investors continued to believe that Japan has abandoned its weak-yen, strong-dollar policy.
The bond market was closed for the Veterans' Day holiday.
The Dow Jones industrial average ended up 35.78 points at 6,255.60, eclipsing Friday's record closing high of 6,219.82.

It was the Dow's longest string of new milestones since the seven-session streak from Feb. 5 to 13. Last week's 198-point post-election rally was the second-biggest weekly point gain ever after the 207-point surge in the week of Aug. 2 this year.

In the broader market, advancing issues led declines 1,391 to 996 on moderate volume of 353 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange, where trading was somewhat muted due to the observance of Veterans' Day.

Other market gauges also set new highs. The Standard & Poor's composite index of 500 stocks rose 1.05 to 731.87, its fifth consecutive record, and the NYSE Composite index of all listed common stocks gained 0.51 to 386.83, a new high.

The technology-studded Nasdaq Composite index rose 5.16 to 1,262.67, topping its Oct. 15 record of 1,258.10 on bullishness prior to release after the close of the Semiconductor Industry Association's book-to-bill report for October.

The stock of computer chip companies surged in anticipation that the closely watched book-to-bill ratio -- a measure of the industry's activity -- would top the 1.0 level for the first time this year.
It came in at 1.10 vs. a revised 0.98 in September and the highest since December 1995's 1.12 level.
A book-to-bill of 1.0 means that for every dollar of computer chips shipped, one dollar of new orders was recorded.
Stocks were bolstered by the prospect that the Federal Reserve will hold monetary policy steady at Wednesday's meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee.

The market also got a shot in the arm after Smith Barney raised the stock portion in its recommended asset allocation to 50 percent from 45 percent, cut cash to 10 percent from 15 percent and kept bonds at 40 percent.

The dollar dropped to 111.00 yen in late trading from 111.73 yen late Friday and hit a one-month intraday low of 110.90 yen. The dollar hit a post-Second World War low of 79.75 yen on April 19, 1995 but has climbed sharply since then.
The dollar fell as low as 1.4910 German marks, its lowest level since 1.4880 marks on Sept. 9. It fetched 1.4935 marks in late trading, down from 1.5047 marks late Friday.

In commodities, soybean futures on the Chicago Board of Trade fell amid fears that a trade dispute with key importer China could escalate. The November contract closed 7-3/4 cents a bushel lower at $6.80.

December copper closed 1.25 cents up at 95.60 cents a pound on expecations that Tuesday's key London Metal Exchange stock data will show a further fall in inventories, which currently stand at a six-year low of 113,400 metric tons.

Overseas, London's FTSE 100 index ended up 3.6 points at 3,914.4 after trading in negative territory for most of the day. In Tokyo, the 225-issue Nikkei average lost 135.96 points, or 0.64 percent, to land at 21,065.08.
